title: Extension Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS0)
summary: Describes backward-compatible extension mechanisms for DNS (EDNS0), since fixed fields in the protocol were running out of room and clients could not announce their abilities. It was replaced by RFC 6891.

eli5.summary: The old address book form had no room left for new details. This added an optional extra page so computers can say what they can handle.

questions: what is the dns opt record
why is the dns udp limit 512 bytes
subtitle: The original way to let DNS messages grow past their fixed limits, built around one optional OPT record.

tldr.problem: DNS had fixed header fields that were running out of values, a 512-octet limit on UDP messages, and no way for clients to tell servers what they can handle.
tldr.mechanism: A single optional OPT pseudo-record in the additional section carries the sender's UDP payload size, an extended response code, a version number and a list of options.
tldr.outcome: It was replaced by RFC 6891, which now defines EDNS(0).

today: RFC 2671 was obsoleted by RFC 6891, which is the current definition of these DNS extension mechanisms.

sections.title: Why DNS Needed Room to Grow
sections.content:
The DNS message format fixes many limits. The RFC points to three that were running out: the flag and response-code bits in the header, the label types at the start of each name label, and the 512-octet limit on messages sent over UDP. Clients also had no way to advertise their capabilities.

Old clients will not understand the new fields. The design therefore has to include a fallback so that new and old software can still work together.
sections.eli5: The old form had only so many boxes to tick, and they were nearly all used up. Computers also could not say what they were able to do.

sections.title: Extended Label Types
sections.content:
The first two bits of a name label say what type of label it is. Only two of the four possible types were in use. The RFC makes the 0 1 type mean an extended label type, with the actual type in the lower six bits of the first octet. All label types developed later should use this scheme.

The extended type 1 1 1 1 1 1 is reserved for expanding the extended type space again.
sections.eli5: When the label types were nearly all taken, one was set aside as a door to a whole new set of types.

sections.title: The OPT Pseudo-Record
sections.content:
The core of the design is the OPT pseudo-RR. A message carries zero or one of them in its additional data section. It is called a pseudo-RR because it describes the message itself, not real DNS data. OPT records must never be cached, forwarded, or stored in or loaded from master files.

Its fixed part reuses the usual record fields: the name is empty (the root), the CLASS field holds the sender's UDP payload size, and the TTL field holds the extended response code and flags. The variable part in RDATA is a list of options, each with an OPTION-CODE, an OPTION-LENGTH and OPTION-DATA.

The TTL field splits into EXTENDED-RCODE (the upper 8 bits of a 12-bit response code), VERSION and a 16-bit Z field. Senders set Z to zero and receivers ignore it. A version of 0 means full conformance with this specification.
sections.eli5: The OPT record is a sticky note attached to a message. It says how big a reply you can read, and it can hold extra requests.

sections.title: Payload Size and Versions
sections.content:
The advertised UDP payload size is the largest UDP payload the sender can reassemble and deliver. The path MTU may be smaller. The RFC says that a 512-octet payload needs a 576-octet IP reassembly buffer and that 1280 would be reasonable for an Ethernet-connected requestor. Too large a value may cause an ICMP message from a gateway or a silent drop of the response.

A requestor's maximum size should not be cached beyond the transaction. A responder's size can reasonably be expected to stay constant between two sequential transactions. Advertising an architectural limit is unwise: a stack that can reassemble 64KB datagrams should not assume it wants to spend more than about 4KB of state per transaction.

If a responder does not implement the requested version, it answers with BADVERS. Each response carries the responder's highest version, so a requestor learns it as a side effect.
sections.eli5: You tell the other side the biggest parcel you can carry. Say a smaller size than your very limit so you do not get overloaded.

sections.title: Fallback and Probing
sections.content:
An OPT record in a request means the requestor fully implements that version of EDNS. A request without one means the responder must not use any of these extensions in its reply.

Responders that do not understand the extensions are expected to answer with NOTIMPL, FORMERR or SERVFAIL. So a requestor should probe, and retry without extensions after one of those codes. If it caches a responder's capability level, it should probe again periodically.
sections.eli5: Try the new way first. If the other side looks confused, say it the old way instead.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The only security concern raised is that a requestor-chosen buffer size could enable a denial of service attack. If responders can be made to send messages too large for intermediate gateways to forward, ICMP storms between gateways and responders could result.

IANA assigned RR type code 41 to OPT. The RFC expands the response code space from 4 bits to 12 bits, assigns extended RCODE 16 to BADVERS, and reserves option code 65535. It recommends registries for extended label types, option codes and version numbers.
sections.eli5: Asking for huge replies could clog the roads between computers, so be careful how big you ask.
